content.title: HTML & CSS
content.subject: coding
content.description: Build the structure of a web page with HTML, then make it look good with CSS. Every lesson ends with a small coding activity that is checked automatically.

items.title: Your first HTML tag
items.body:
Every web page is written in **HTML** (HyperText Markup Language). HTML describes *what* is on a page using **tags**. Most tags come in pairs: an opening tag like `

` and a closing tag like `

`. Whatever goes between them is the content. Together they form an **element**. ~~~

This is a big heading

~~~ `h1` stands for "heading level 1", the most important title on the page.
items.task: Write an `<h1>` element that contains the text `Hello, world!`
items.starter: <!-- Write your h1 element below this line -->
items.solution: Hello, world!
items.hint:
Open with

, write the text, then close with

. Don't forget the slash in the closing tag.

items.body:
HTML has six heading levels, `

` through `

`. Use them like the outline of a document: one `

` tag: ~~~

Today I started learning to code.

It was fun!

~~~ Browsers ignore extra spaces and line breaks in your code, so each paragraph needs its own `

` tag.

items.title: Links & images
items.body: Tags can have **attributes**: extra settings written inside the opening tag as `name="value"`. A **link** uses the `` (anchor) tag. Its `href` attribute says where the link goes: ~~~ Read the docs ~~~ An **image** uses ``. It has no closing tag, because it has no text content. `src` is the image address, and `alt` describes the image for people using screen readers (and for when the image fails to load): ~~~ ~~~

items.title: Classes & the box model
items.body:
To style only *some* elements, give them a **class** and select it with a dot: ~~~
I am a card
~~~ `
` is a generic container with no meaning of its own, which makes it perfect for layout. ## The box model Every element is a box with layers, from the inside out: - **content**: the text or image - **padding**: space inside the border - **border**: a line around the box, e.g. `border: 2px solid black;` - **margin**: space outside, pushing other elements away

content.title: JavaScript
content.subject: coding
content.description: Learn to program with JavaScript: variables, functions, decisions, loops and data. Write real code and see it run instantly.

items.title: Hello, console
items.body:
**JavaScript** is the programming language of the web. A program is a list of instructions that the computer runs from top to bottom.

The easiest way to see what your program is doing is `console.log`, which prints a value to the console:

~~~
console.log("I am learning JavaScript");
console.log(2 + 3);
~~~

Text values are called **strings** and go inside quotes. Numbers don't need quotes. Press **Run** (or **Ctrl + Enter**) to see the output.
items.task: Log exactly `Hello, World!` to the console.
items.starter: // Lines starting with // are comments. The computer ignores them.
items.solution: console.log("Hello, World!");
items.hint: Use console.log("Hello, World!"). Check the capital letters, the comma and the exclamation mark.

items.title: Variables
items.body:
A **variable** is a named box that stores a value so you can use it later.

~~~
const city = "Lisbon";   // const: can't be reassigned
let score = 10;          // let: can change later
score = score + 5;
console.log(city, score); // Lisbon 15
~~~

Use `const` by default and `let` only when the value needs to change. Names are case-sensitive, so `score` and `Score` are different variables.
items.task: Create a `const` called `myName` holding your name (a string), and a `let` called `age` holding a number. Then add 1 to `age` and log both variables.
items.hint: const myName = "Ada"; let age = 36; age = age + 1; console.log(myName, age);

checks.label: myName is declared with const and age with let

items.title: Strings & template literals
items.task: Create `const firstName = "Ada"`. Then use a **template literal** to create `greeting` equal to `Hello, Ada!`, and log it.
items.starter: const firstName = "Ada";
items.hint: const greeting = `Hello, ${firstName}!`;  (those are backticks, the key left of 1 on most keyboards)

items.title: Functions
items.task: Write a function `add(a, b)` that **returns** the sum of its two parameters.
items.hint: Inside the function body, write: return a + b;

items.title: Making decisions
items.task: Write `grade(score)` that returns `"A"` for 90 and up, `"B"` for 80–89, `"C"` for 70–79, and `"F"` for anything lower.
items.hint: Check the highest grade first: if (score >= 90) return "A"; then else if (score >= 80)…

items.title: Loops
items.task: Write `sumTo(n)` that uses a loop to return the sum of all whole numbers from 1 to `n`. For example, `sumTo(4)` is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.
items.hint: for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) { total += i; }

items.title: Arrays
items.task: Write `largest(nums)` that returns the biggest number in an array, **without** using `Math.max`. Assume the array has at least one number.
items.hint: Loop over nums. If the current number is greater than biggest, replace biggest with it.

checks.label: Biggest at the end: largest([1, 2, 30]) is 30

items.title: Objects
items.body:
An **object** groups related values together under named **keys**:

~~~
const pet = {
  name: "Biscuit",
  species: "dog",
  age: 4,
};

console.log(pet.name);   // "Biscuit"
pet.age = 5;             // update a value
~~~

Objects are perfect for describing *things*: a user, a product, a book. You can pass them into functions just like any other value.
items.task: Create an object `book` with keys `title` (string), `author` (string) and `pages` (number). Then write `describe(b)` that returns a string like `"Dune by Frank Herbert"` for any book object.
items.hint: Use b.title and b.author inside a template literal: `${b.title} by ${b.author}`

checks.label: book has a string title and author
checks.test: typeof book.title === 'string' && book.title.length > 0 && typeof book.author === 'string' && book.author.length > 0

checks.label: describe works for other books too
checks.test: describe({ title: 'Emma', author: 'Jane Austen', pages: 400 }) === 'Emma by Jane Austen'

items.title: Array methods: map & filter
items.body:
Arrays have built-in methods that take a function and apply it to every item.

`filter` keeps only the items where your function returns `true`:

~~~
const ages = [12, 25, 17, 40];
const adults = ages.filter(age => age >= 18); // [25, 40]
~~~

`map` transforms every item into something new:

~~~
const doubled = [1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2); // [2, 4, 6]
~~~

`n => n * 2` is an **arrow function**, a short way to write a function. You can **chain** methods: `nums.filter(...).map(...)`.

A number is even when `n % 2 === 0` (`%` gives the remainder after dividing).
items.task: Write `evensDoubled(nums)` that keeps only the **even** numbers and then **doubles** each one. `evensDoubled([1, 2, 3, 4])` should return `[4, 8]`.
items.hint: return nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0).map(n => n * 2);

checks.label: Does not change the original array

items.title: Challenge: FizzBuzz
items.body:
Time to combine everything! **FizzBuzz** is a classic programming puzzle.

For each number from 1 to `n`:

- if it's divisible by **both 3 and 5**, use `"FizzBuzz"`
- otherwise, if divisible by **3**, use `"Fizz"`
- otherwise, if divisible by **5**, use `"Buzz"`
- otherwise, use the number itself **as a string**, e.g. `"7"`

You'll need a loop, `if` statements, the `%` operator, and an array with `push`. Tip: think about which check has to come first. Turn a number into a string with `String(7)`.
items.task: Write `fizzbuzz(n)` that returns an **array of strings** following the rules above. `fizzbuzz(5)` is `["1", "2", "Fizz", "4", "Buzz"]`.
items.hint: Check "divisible by 15" (both 3 and 5) FIRST, otherwise 15 would be caught by the "divisible by 3" check.

checks.label: Position 30 is "FizzBuzz", 9 is "Fizz", 10 is "Buzz"
checks.test: (() => { const r = fizzbuzz(30); return r[29] === 'FizzBuzz' && r[8] === 'Fizz' && r[9] === 'Buzz'; })()

content.title: Fractions Made Simple
content.description: Understand what fractions mean, find equivalent fractions and compare them, using pizzas, rulers and everyday objects.
content.subject: math

items.title: What is a fraction?
items.body:
A **fraction** describes part of a whole. It has two numbers:

- the **denominator** (bottom) says how many equal parts the whole is split into
- the **numerator** (top) says how many of those parts you have

If a pizza is cut into 8 equal slices and you eat 3, you ate `3/8` of the pizza.

## Equal parts matter
The parts must be the **same size**. Cutting a pizza into one huge slice and seven tiny ones does not make eighths.

## Fractions on a number line
Fractions are numbers too. `1/2` sits halfway between 0 and 1, and `4/4` is exactly 1.

items.title: Equivalent fractions
items.body:
Different fractions can name the **same amount**. Half a pizza is `1/2`, but it is also `2/4` and `4/8`.

## Making equivalent fractions
Multiply (or divide) the top **and** bottom by the same number:

~~~
1/2 = (1×3)/(2×3) = 3/6
6/8 = (6÷2)/(8÷2) = 3/4
~~~

## Simplest form
A fraction is in **simplest form** when no number other than 1 divides both the top and bottom. `3/4` is simplest; `6/8` is not.

items.title: Comparing fractions
items.body:
To compare two fractions, give them the **same denominator** first.

Which is bigger, `2/3` or `3/4`?

~~~
2/3 = 8/12
3/4 = 9/12
~~~

`9/12` is more than `8/12`, so `3/4` is bigger.

## A shortcut
When the numerators are the same, the fraction with the **smaller** denominator is bigger: `1/3` is more than `1/5` because each piece is larger.

items.title: Activity: fraction hunt
items.body:
Fractions are everywhere. Time to find some!

- Look at a measuring cup, a ruler, a clock or a recipe.
- Find **three** real fractions and note where you saw them.
- For one of them, write an equivalent fraction.
items.task: Write down the three fractions you found, where you found them, and one equivalent fraction.

items.title: Fractions quiz
items.body: Show what you know. You need **70%** to pass.

questions.prompt: In 3/8, what does the 8 tell you?
choices: How many equal parts make the whole
questions.explanation: The denominator is the number of equal parts in the whole.

questions.prompt: Which fraction is equivalent to 1/2?
questions.explanation: Multiply top and bottom of 1/2 by 3 to get 3/6.

questions.prompt: What is 6/8 in simplest form?
questions.explanation: Divide top and bottom by 2.

questions.prompt: Which is bigger?
Which is bigger?
questions.explanation: With the same numerator, the smaller denominator means bigger pieces.

content.title: Our Solar System
content.description: Tour the Sun, the eight planets and what makes each one special, then build a scale model of how far apart they really are.
content.subject: science

items.title: The Sun and its family
items.body:
Our **solar system** is the Sun and everything that orbits it: eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets like Pluto, asteroids and comets.

## The Sun
The Sun is a **star**, a giant ball of hot gas. It holds more than 99% of all the mass in the solar system, and its **gravity** keeps everything in orbit.

## Orbits
An **orbit** is the path an object takes around another. Earth takes about **365 days** to orbit the Sun once: that is one year.

items.title: Rocky planets and gas giants
items.body:
The planets, in order from the Sun: **Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune**.

## The rocky planets
The four inner planets are small with solid, rocky surfaces. Venus is the **hottest** planet because its thick atmosphere traps heat.

## The giants
The four outer planets are huge and mostly gas or ice. **Jupiter** is the largest: more than 1,300 Earths would fit inside it. Saturn's famous rings are made of ice and rock.

## Remember the order
Try: *My Very Excellent Mother Just Served Us Nachos.*

items.title: Activity: build a scale model
items.body:
Space is mostly empty. Let's see how empty!

Using **1 step = 10 million km**, the planets are roughly this many steps from the Sun:

~~~
Mercury 6   Venus 11   Earth 15   Mars 23
Jupiter 78  Saturn 143  Uranus 287  Neptune 450
~~~

- Put an object outside to be the Sun.
- Walk out and drop a marker (a stone, a note) at each planet.
- Look back at the Sun from Neptune.
items.task: Describe your model. What surprised you about the distances?

items.title: Solar system quiz
items.body: Test your knowledge. You need **70%** to pass.

questions.prompt: What keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
questions.explanation: The Sun's gravity pulls on every planet.

questions.prompt: Which planet is the largest?
questions.explanation: Jupiter is the biggest planet by far.

questions.prompt: Which planet is the hottest?
questions.explanation: Venus's thick atmosphere traps heat, making it hotter than Mercury.

questions.prompt: About how long does Earth take to orbit the Sun?
questions.explanation: One orbit is one year.

content.title: Programming Fundamentals
content.description: The ideas behind every programming language: algorithms, variables, data types, decisions, loops, functions and debugging. Practise each one by writing real code.
content.subject: coding
objectives: Explain what a program and an algorithm are
Store and change information with variables
Make decisions with if / else and repeat work with loops
Write functions and find bugs in your own code

items.title: What is a program?
items.body:
A **program** is a list of instructions that a computer follows, one after another. Computers are fast, but they are not clever: they do *exactly* what you say, nothing more.

## Input, process, output
Almost every program follows the same pattern:

- **Input:** information goes in (a key press, a tap, a number)
- **Process:** the program works with it (adds, compares, sorts)
- **Output:** a result comes out (text on screen, a sound, a saved file)

A calculator app takes two numbers as input, adds them as the process, and shows the answer as output.

## Programming languages
We write instructions in a **programming language** such as Python, JavaScript or C++. They look different, but they share the same big ideas, and that's what this course teaches. The practice activities use JavaScript because it runs right here in your browser.

items.title: Algorithms and pseudocode
items.body:
An **algorithm** is a step-by-step plan to solve a problem. A recipe is an algorithm. So are the directions to your school.

Good algorithms are **precise** (no guessing), **ordered** (steps happen in the right order) and **finish** (they don't go on forever).

## Pseudocode
Before writing real code, programmers often plan with **pseudocode**: plain-language steps that look a bit like code.

~~~
SET total TO 0
FOR EACH price IN shopping list
    ADD price TO total
END FOR
SHOW total
~~~

Pseudocode has no strict rules. Its job is to make your thinking clear, so turning it into any programming language is easy.

items.title: Activity: the robot sandwich
items.body:
Computers follow instructions literally. Let's feel what that's like!

- Write an algorithm for something everyday, like making a sandwich or drawing a house.
- Give it to a friend or family member. They must act like a robot and do **exactly** what each step says, nothing more.
- Watch where it goes wrong, then fix your steps and try again.
items.task: Write your final algorithm, then describe one step that went wrong the first time and how you fixed it.

items.title: Variables
items.task: Create a variable `player` holding your name (a string) and a variable `score` holding the number `100`. Then log a sentence that uses both.

checks.label: player is a string with your name
Logs a sentence that includes the score

items.title: Data types
items.body:
Every value has a **type**, and the type decides what you can do with it.

- **Number:** `42`, `3.14` (you can do math with them)
- **String:** `"hello"` (text, written in quotes)
- **Boolean:** `true` or `false` (yes / no answers)
- **List (array):** `["red", "green", "blue"]` (many values in order)

Types matter! In JavaScript, `"5" + 1` gives `"51"` because adding to a string joins text. But `5 + 1` gives `6`.

## Comparisons give booleans
~~~
7 > 3      // true
2 === 5    // false
"cat" === "cat"   // true
~~~

items.title: Debugging: find the bugs
items.body:
A **bug** is a mistake in code. **Debugging** means finding and fixing it. Professional programmers spend lots of time doing this, so it's a skill worth practising!

## A debugging routine
- Read the error message: it often names the line
- Use `console.log` to check what values really are
- Change one thing at a time, then run again
items.task: This program should add up the numbers in `prices` and log `Total: 15`, but it has **two bugs**. Find and fix them.
items.hint: Lists start counting at 0, not 1. And check the spelling of total in the last line.

content.title: Python Basics
content.description: Learn Python, one of the world's most popular languages: printing, variables, strings, decisions, lists, loops and functions, with plenty of predict-the-output practice.
content.subject: coding
objectives: Write Python programs that print, store and combine values
Use if / elif / else and indentation correctly
Work with lists and repeat code with for and while loops
Organise code into functions with parameters and return values

items.title: Meet Python
items.body:
**Python** is a programming language known for being easy to read. It's used for websites, games, science, robots and artificial intelligence.

Here is a complete Python program:

~~~
# This line is a comment. Python ignores it.
print("Hello, World!")
print(7 + 3)
~~~

It prints two lines: `Hello, World!` and `10`.

## How to run Python
Install Python from python.org (or ask an adult to), then use the editor that comes with it, called **IDLE**, or a beginner editor like **Thonny**. Both work without internet once installed. You can also do every activity in this course with pen and paper by predicting what the code will do.

items.title: Variables and types
items.body:
Variables store values. In Python you just pick a name and use `=`:

~~~
name = "Ada"
age = 12
height = 1.52
likes_coding = True

print(name, "is", age)
print(type(height))
~~~

## The four basic types
- `int`: whole numbers like `12`
- `float`: decimals like `1.52`
- `str`: text in quotes like `"Ada"`
- `bool`: `True` or `False` (capital letters in Python!)

Variable names can't have spaces, so Python programmers use underscores: `likes_coding`.

items.title: Strings, f-strings and input
items.body:
Strings are text. You can join them with `+` and repeat them with a number:

~~~
greeting = "Hi " + "there"
print(greeting)        # Hi there
print("ha" * 3)        # hahaha
print(len("Python"))   # 6
~~~

## f-strings
Put `f` before the quotes and you can drop variables straight into text with `{ }`:

~~~
name = "Ada"
age = 12
print(f"{name} is {age} years old")
~~~

## Asking the user
`input()` waits for the user to type something. It always gives back a **string**, so use `int()` to turn it into a number:

~~~
year = int(input("What year were you born? "))
print(f"In 2030 you will be {2030 - year}")
~~~

items.title: Predict the output
items.body: Read each line of code and predict what Python prints. You need **70%** to pass, and you can retry as often as you like.

questions.prompt: What does `print(3 + 4 * 2)` show?
questions.explanation: Multiplication happens first: 4 × 2 = 8, then 3 + 8 = 11.

questions.prompt: What does `print("3" + "4")` show?
questions.explanation: Adding two strings joins them together.

questions.prompt: What does `print(len("cow"))` show?
questions.explanation: len counts the characters in a string.

questions.prompt: name = "Moo" — what does `print(f"Hi {name}!")` show?
questions.explanation: An f-string swaps {name} for the variable's value.

questions.prompt: What type does `input()` always return?
questions.explanation: input() gives text, so convert it with int() for math.

items.title: Making decisions: if, elif, else
items.body:
Python uses `if`, `elif` (else if) and `else` to choose what to do:

~~~
score = 72

if score >= 90:
    print("Amazing!")
elif score >= 60:
    print("You passed")
else:
    print("Keep practising")
~~~

This prints `You passed`. Python checks each condition from the top and runs the **first** one that's true.

## Indentation matters
In Python, the lines that belong to an `if` must be **indented** (usually 4 spaces), and the `if` line ends with a colon `:`. Forgetting either one is the most common beginner error.

## Comparisons
~~~
==   equal to          !=   not equal to
>    greater than      <    less than
>=   at least          <=   at most
~~~

Combine conditions with `and`, `or` and `not`: `if age >= 13 and age <= 19:`

items.title: Lists
items.body:
A **list** stores many values in order, inside square brackets:

~~~
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
print(fruits[0])      # apple
print(fruits[-1])     # cherry
print(len(fruits))    # 3

fruits.append("mango")
fruits[1] = "kiwi"
print(fruits)         # ['apple', 'kiwi', 'cherry', 'mango']
~~~

## Counting starts at 0
The first item is at **index 0**, the second at index 1, and so on. Negative numbers count from the end, so `-1` is the last item.

Check whether something is in a list with `in`: `if "apple" in fruits:`

items.title: Loops: for and while
items.body:
A `for` loop goes through each item in a list, or through a range of numbers:

~~~
for fruit in ["apple", "kiwi"]:
    print("I like", fruit)

for i in range(3):
    print(i)        # 0, 1, 2

for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)        # 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
~~~

`range(3)` gives 0, 1, 2: it stops **before** the end number.

## while loops
A `while` loop repeats as long as a condition is true:

~~~
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1
print("Lift off!")
~~~

Make sure something changes inside the loop, or it will run forever!

items.title: Functions
items.body:
A **function** is a named block of code you can reuse. Create one with `def`:

~~~
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

greet("Ada")
greet("Moo")
~~~

## Returning a value
`return` sends a result back so you can use it:

~~~
def area(width, height):
    return width * height

room = area(4, 3)
print(room)    # 12
~~~

`width` and `height` are **parameters**: the inputs a function needs. Functions keep programs tidy: write the code once, use it everywhere.

items.title: Activity: build a guessing game
items.body:
Time to combine everything! Here's the plan for a number-guessing game:

~~~
import random
secret = random.randint(1, 20)
guesses = 0

while True:
    guess = int(input("Guess a number from 1 to 20: "))
    guesses = guesses + 1
    if guess < secret:
        print("Too low!")
    elif guess > secret:
        print("Too high!")
    else:
        print(f"You got it in {guesses} guesses!")
        break
~~~

- If you have Python installed, type it in and play it. Otherwise, play it on paper with a friend acting as the computer.
- Then **change it**: try a bigger range, a limit of 5 guesses, or a message when the guess is very close.

items.title: Your first C++ program
Variables and types
items.body:
In C++, you must say a variable's **type** when you create it:

~~~
int lives = 3;              // whole number
double speed = 2.5;         // decimal number
char grade = 'A';           // one character, single quotes
bool gameOver = false;      // true or false
std::string name = "Moo";   // text (needs #include <string>)
~~~

The type can't change later: `lives` will always hold whole numbers.

## Watch out: integer division
When you divide two `int`s, C++ throws away the decimal part:

~~~
std::cout << 7 / 2;     // 3, not 3.5!
std::cout << 7.0 / 2;   // 3.5
std::cout << 7 % 2;     // 1 (the remainder)
~~~
